frictionVectors.title: European Energy Transition
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong control over gas exports and pipeline infrastructure, but Europe’s diversification and long-term decarbonization could reduce future leverage and revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Border Instability
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Libya, and Niger increases pressure on Algeria’s southern borders and complicates its non-interventionist regional posture.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor is attracting U.S., European, Chinese, and Gulf interest, creating bargaining opportunities but also pressure over transport, mining, and strategic access.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Revenue Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Angola retains formal control over its oil sector, yet declining production, foreign-operator dependence, and price volatility constrain sovereign fiscal autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Niger Transit Disruption
frictionVectors.details: Political tensions with Niger have exposed Benin’s dependence on cross-border trade and highlighted the vulnerability of Cotonou-linked transport infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Insurgent Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Armed-group activity near the northern frontier is increasing security costs and threatening roads, parks, and energy infrastructure connected to regional commerce.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond Market Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Botswana has strengthened its negotiating position with major diamond partners, but remains exposed to weak global demand, synthetic stones, and concentration in a single export sector.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Energy and Water Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Limited domestic generation and water stress increase reliance on regional infrastructure and imported inputs, constraining full sovereign control over industrial expansion.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-Sector Externalization
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking greater state control over gold production, but foreign-linked operators, informal exports, and opaque security arrangements continue to capture significant value.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Growing reliance on Russian security support may reduce Western influence while creating new political, financial, and resource-access dependencies.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque Mining Renegotiations
frictionVectors.details: Bujumbura is seeking tighter state control over gold, nickel, and rare-mineral operations, but weak oversight and opaque contract processes leave room for foreign and politically connected actors to capture rents.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda–Burundi Security Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Mutual accusations over armed groups and cross-border support keep the frontier unstable, threatening trade corridors and limiting Burundi's ability to manage regional infrastructure independently.

frictionVectors.title: External Dependence on Ports and Finance
frictionVectors.details: Praia benefits from European, American, and Chinese interest in Atlantic logistics, but dependence on external capital and tourism constrains bargaining power over strategic port and connectivity assets.

frictionVectors.title: Atlantic Maritime Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Drug trafficking, illegal fishing, and competition over maritime surveillance require outside security support, creating a persistent trade-off between sovereignty and operational dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Energy and Mining
frictionVectors.details: Oil, gas, timber, and emerging mining projects remain heavily dependent on foreign capital and operators, while Chinese-backed infrastructure finance can increase state liabilities and reduce negotiating room.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone and Gulf of Guinea Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: The Anglophone conflict and piracy risks around the Gulf of Guinea weaken state control over transport corridors, ports, and productive regions, inviting expanded external security involvement.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security and Mining Influence
frictionVectors.details: Russian security personnel and aligned commercial networks remain central to regime protection and access to gold and diamond zones, limiting Bangui's independent control over strategic resources.

frictionVectors.title: Borderland Conflict and Informal Extraction
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups and cross-border trafficking linked to Sudan, Chad, and neighboring states disrupt roads and mining areas, allowing external networks to extract value outside formal state channels.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Dependence in Oil Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chad's fiscal and export capacity remains tied to foreign-operated oil production and pipeline infrastructure, leaving the state vulnerable to contract disputes, financing pressure, and external leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan Border and Gold-Network Exposure
frictionVectors.details: The Sudan conflict is intensifying refugee, arms, and illicit-gold flows across eastern Chad, stretching state capacity and increasing the influence of regional security and commercial actors.

frictionVectors.title: French Control of Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: France retains effective control of Mayotte, sustaining a central sovereignty dispute and limiting Comoros' leverage over surrounding maritime resources. The issue also drives migration tensions and periodic diplomatic escalation.

frictionVectors.title: External Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Comoros relies heavily on remittances, foreign aid, and imported fuel, leaving fiscal and energy security vulnerable to outside actors. Limited state capacity constrains independent management of maritime and fisheries assets.

frictionVectors.title: M23 and Regional Intervention
frictionVectors.details: Conflict involving M23, Rwanda, and regional forces continues to weaken Kinshasa's control over eastern territory and transport corridors. Displacement and insecurity obstruct formal taxation and local resource governance.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: Cobalt, copper, and other strategic minerals attract intense competition from Chinese, Western, and regional investors. Contract renegotiations and artisanal mining reforms have improved leverage rhetorically, but enforcement and value capture remain limited.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Oil remains the backbone of state revenue, exposing sovereignty and public investment to price volatility and the bargaining power of foreign operators. Diversification and transparent management of petroleum income remain weak.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-Linked Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, ports, and energy projects expand connectivity but can narrow fiscal and contractual room for maneuver. Infrastructure access and repayment obligations remain central to Brazzaville's external relationships.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa and Commodity Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire is strengthening domestic processing and producer oversight, but foreign buyers and volatile global prices still capture substantial value. Climate stress and aging plantations threaten long-term resource security.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Security Competition
frictionVectors.details: Abidjan's port and logistics expansion increases national leverage while attracting competition from Gulf, Chinese, European, and regional investors. Spillover from Sahel instability continues to pressure northern infrastructure and defense spending.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military Footprint
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti monetizes its position near the Bab el-Mandeb through multiple foreign military facilities, gaining revenue and security but accepting constrained strategic autonomy. Regional crises can rapidly raise pressure on its ports and territory.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Port Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed infrastructure and Ethiopia-linked transport revenues provide economic leverage while increasing exposure to debt, traffic volatility, and external bargaining. Control over port assets and corridor terms remains a persistent sovereignty concern.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Asset Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Heavy external financing needs have increased reliance on Gulf capital, multilateral lenders, and asset sales. This can dilute domestic control over strategic land, ports, and infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea and Canal Security
frictionVectors.details: Regional conflict and attacks near the Red Sea continue to threaten Suez Canal traffic and revenue. Egypt retains sovereign control of the canal but remains exposed to external security dynamics.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Oil and gas production, technology, and marketing remain dependent on foreign operators and external capital. Falling output heightens pressure to monetize new offshore resources and LNG infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque Infrastructure Finance
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign contractors have played major roles in transport and public works. Debt transparency and limited domestic participation constrain the state’s effective control over long-term infrastructure value.

frictionVectors.title: External Port Competition
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea’s Red Sea coastline gives it strategic leverage, but regional competition involving Ethiopia, Gulf states, and international naval actors creates persistent sovereignty risks around ports and maritime access.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Mining
frictionVectors.details: Mining remains a major source of foreign exchange and is reliant on external operators and financing. Limited transparency and sanctions exposure reduce domestic bargaining power over resource development.

frictionVectors.title: South African Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Trade routes, electricity, finance, and supply chains are heavily tied to South Africa and the Southern African Customs Union. This provides stability but sharply limits independent economic maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Preferential Market Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Sugar, apparel, and forestry depend on external market access and trade preferences. Changes in regional or Western trade regimes could quickly weaken fiscal and employment stability.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Basin Tensions
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam strengthens Ethiopia’s control over national power and water infrastructure but remains a major point of friction with Egypt and Sudan. Disputes over filling and drought operations remain unresolved.

frictionVectors.title: External Finance and Connectivity
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and the need for foreign investment constrain Addis Ababa’s control over infrastructure and strategic sectors. Gulf, Chinese, and Western partners compete for influence over ports, logistics, energy, and digital systems.

frictionVectors.title: Post-Coup Resource Rebalancing
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are seeking greater state participation and local value capture in oil, manganese, and infrastructure projects. This creates friction with established foreign operators and financiers, particularly where contracts are being reviewed.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign firms remain important to mining, transport, and construction capacity. Libreville is attempting to diversify partnerships without losing access to capital or operational expertise.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Financing Exposure
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia remains reliant on external budget support, concessional finance, and development assistance for infrastructure and public services. Fiscal dependence limits policy autonomy even as authorities seek stricter oversight of external projects.

frictionVectors.title: Senegal Border and Fisheries Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Cross-border trade, security coordination, and access to fisheries are closely tied to Senegal. Maritime resource disputes and informal commerce periodically test Banjul's ability to enforce sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal Mining and Gold Governance
frictionVectors.details: Illegal mining continues to damage waterways, farmland, and state revenue collection, while gold-sector reforms aim to increase domestic participation and formalize trading. The government faces resistance from entrenched networks and local economic interests.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Ghana is seeking better terms and more domestic processing in emerging lithium and other critical-mineral projects. Competition among foreign investors is creating leverage, but financing and technical-capacity constraints remain significant.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Bauxite and the developing Simandou iron-ore complex are dominated by large foreign-led consortia requiring rail, port, and power infrastructure. Conakry is pressing for downstream processing and stronger state returns, but remains dependent on external capital and expertise.

frictionVectors.title: Junta Legitimacy and Contract Risk
frictionVectors.details: The military-led government uses resource nationalism to strengthen domestic legitimacy while delaying a full return to civilian rule. Political uncertainty raises the risk of contract renegotiation, sanctions pressure, and investor caution.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew Export Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains heavily dependent on raw cashew exports, leaving farmers and state revenues exposed to foreign buyers, price swings, and limited domestic processing. Attempts to build local value chains are constrained by weak power, transport, and finance systems.

frictionVectors.title: Political Instability and Trafficking Risk
frictionVectors.details: Institutional fragility and recurring political confrontation weaken control over ports, borders, and customs. International security partners remain important in countering illicit trafficking and organized crime, limiting autonomous enforcement capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Rail and port-linked debt obligations continue to shape fiscal choices, although Nairobi retains meaningful bargaining leverage through diversified Gulf, Western, and Asian partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Critical minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms and governments are positioning for access to Kenya's emerging mineral and renewable-energy supply chains, creating pressure for stronger local-processing and transparency rules.

frictionVectors.title: South African water leverage
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water exports and infrastructure are deeply tied to South Africa, limiting Maseru's autonomy despite the strategic value of its mountain watershed.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of mining value
frictionVectors.details: The diamond sector attracts external capital while domestic processing and fiscal capture remain limited, leaving the country vulnerable to commodity cycles and concession disputes.

highlights: Ports and concessions draw strategic interest

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore concession dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large foreign-backed mining projects dominate expectations for growth, but transport, power, and revenue-sharing arrangements determine whether Liberia captures durable national value.

frictionVectors.title: Port and coastal competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investors and regional actors are seeking influence over port, logistics, and agricultural assets, increasing pressure on Monrovia to strengthen concession oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Competing control of oil infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Rival authorities and armed networks continue to contest terminals, fields, and revenue channels, while foreign partners use energy access to reinforce political influence.

frictionVectors.title: Mercenary and border influence
frictionVectors.details: External military support and security competition around southern borders constrain Libya's ability to secure transport routes, energy assets, and independent foreign policy.

highlights: Nickel and cobalt anchor foreign leverage

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector concentration
frictionVectors.details: Large foreign-backed nickel, cobalt, and ilmenite operations provide exports and jobs but leave Madagascar exposed to commodity swings, energy costs, and disputes over fiscal and environmental terms.

frictionVectors.title: Resource corridors and land pressure
frictionVectors.details: Roads, ports, and power projects linked to mining and agriculture can improve connectivity while intensifying concerns over land rights, local consent, and unequal value capture.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Leverage
frictionVectors.details: IMF-backed reforms and creditor negotiations are narrowing Malawi's policy space. Fiscal pressure may accelerate concessions in mining, energy, and infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Minerals Governance
frictionVectors.details: Uranium and emerging rare-earth projects could improve export earnings, but limited state capacity and foreign capital dependence create risks around contract transparency and local value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Gold Contract Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are seeking a larger state share of gold revenues and tighter oversight of foreign operators. The approach strengthens bargaining power but risks investment disruption and opaque elite capture.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-linked security forces expands Bamako's room to resist Western pressure but introduces accountability concerns, civilian-protection risks, and a new external dependency.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Energy Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim gas project and related infrastructure remain heavily dependent on international partners and export markets. Mauritania is gaining revenue and leverage, but domestic processing and technology transfer remain limited.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and Transit Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Iron-ore expansion and proposed hydrogen projects could diversify the economy, while Chinese, Gulf, and European participation may shape corridor priorities more than local industrial policy.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Connectivity Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius is navigating competition among India, China, Gulf investors, and Western partners over ports, logistics, and digital infrastructure. The government retains meaningful room to balance these relationships.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Finance Scrutiny
frictionVectors.details: International tax and anti-money-laundering standards continue to pressure the offshore financial sector. Compliance costs are rising, but institutional capacity has limited the risk of major external control.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Contest
frictionVectors.details: Control and investment in Western Sahara remain central to Morocco's sovereignty strategy, while diplomatic recognition and legal disputes continue to complicate resource projects and trade routes.

frictionVectors.title: External Capital in Strategic Sectors
frictionVectors.details: European, Gulf, Chinese, and American investment is expanding in ports, automotive manufacturing, renewables, and defense-linked infrastructure. Rabat generally retains strong negotiating control, but exposure to foreign technology and markets remains significant.

highlights: Cabo Delgado security remains the gateway to LNG recovery
Gas wealth is advancing faster than local benefit-sharing

frictionVectors.title: LNG Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign energy companies and security partners remain central to restarting major LNG projects in Cabo Delgado. This limits Maputo's operational autonomy while insurgency risks persist.

frictionVectors.title: Resource-Revenue Governance
frictionVectors.details: Delayed gas revenues, opaque contracting, and uneven provincial development continue to fuel concern that hydrocarbons will primarily benefit external firms and central elites.

highlights: Offshore oil discoveries are reshaping national bargaining power
Green hydrogen ambitions face infrastructure and water constraints

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: International oil majors bring capital and technology to Namibia's frontier discoveries, but local-content demands and state participation will determine how much value remains domestically.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrogen Export Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large green-hydrogen projects depend on foreign finance, imported equipment, port capacity, and export markets. Land, water, and community-consultation pressures could slow implementation.

highlights: The junta is reclaiming control over strategic extractive assets
Sanctions and insecurity constrain the value of resource sovereignty

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Niamey is pressing foreign operators to revise mining terms and assert greater state control, but technical dependence, market access, and legal disputes remain significant constraints.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Corridor Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence threatens roads, power links, and mining logistics. Reduced Western engagement and reliance on alternative security partners have increased uncertainty around infrastructure protection.

highlights: Oil-sector reform is improving formal state leverage
Energy insecurity still undermines resource sovereignty

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital and Oil Output
frictionVectors.details: International operators remain important to offshore production and technical capacity, while regulatory uncertainty, theft, and contract disputes limit Nigeria's ability to capture full value.

frictionVectors.title: Gas and Power Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Pipeline vandalism, underinvestment, and unreliable electricity constrain domestic processing of hydrocarbons. Export-oriented infrastructure continues to outpace dependable supply to Nigerian consumers.

highlights: Kigali is tightening control over mineral-trading channels
Regional security influence is colliding with sovereignty concerns

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo Mineral Flows
frictionVectors.details: Allegations that minerals from eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo transit through Rwanda create sustained diplomatic and sanctions exposure. Kigali rejects responsibility for illicit networks and cites security imperatives.

frictionVectors.title: External Aid and Security Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's security partnerships and donor relationships provide strategic leverage but also expose Kigali to conditionality over regional conduct, governance, and human-rights concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Exploration Dependence
frictionVectors.details: São Tomé and Príncipe relies heavily on foreign capital and technical expertise for offshore exploration, while commercial discoveries remain uncertain. Licensing transparency and revenue safeguards are central sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime Security
frictionVectors.details: The country's strategic position in the Gulf of Guinea attracts security and maritime-sector engagement from external powers. Limited domestic capacity constrains independent enforcement of its maritime claims.

highlights: Gas and oil production reshapes leverage

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Governance
frictionVectors.details: New offshore oil and gas revenues could strengthen fiscal autonomy, but foreign operators, financing structures, and cost-recovery terms limit immediate domestic control. Managing expectations and contract transparency remains politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Fishing Access
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fleets, including European and Asian operators, continue to generate tensions over depleted stocks, licensing, and enforcement. Small-scale fishing communities view opaque access arrangements as a direct threat to food and livelihood security.

frictionVectors.title: External Maritime Footprint
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles depends on partners such as India, France, and other international actors for maritime surveillance and security infrastructure. This improves control over its vast exclusive economic zone but creates balancing concerns around strategic access.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Tourism concentration and infrastructure financing leave the country sensitive to external creditors and climate shocks. Port, connectivity, and coastal-development projects require careful screening to preserve policy autonomy.

highlights: Mining drives growth and bargaining power

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore and Mineral Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-controlled mining remains central to export earnings, employment, and infrastructure promises, leaving Sierra Leone exposed to commodity cycles and uneven value capture. Local-content enforcement and environmental oversight remain contested.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Financing
frictionVectors.details: External investors are important to port, road, and logistics development, but large concessions can create long-term fiscal and strategic dependencies. The government faces pressure to secure transparent terms and domestic processing benefits.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Security Architecture
frictionVectors.details: Somalia remains dependent on external military, financial, and intelligence support to contain al-Shabaab and protect major transport corridors. This assistance is essential but limits autonomous control over security priorities and state-building decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Ports and Maritime Claims
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf states, neighboring countries, and other partners compete for influence over ports, logistics, and maritime security. Offshore resource prospects and tensions involving Ethiopia and Somaliland further raise the stakes around territorial and sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: ENERGY AND LOGISTICS BOTTLENECKS
frictionVectors.details: Persistent weaknesses at Eskom and Transnet limit South Africa's ability to process and export resources on sovereign terms. Private capital and foreign operators are gaining leverage over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: CRITICAL-MINERALS COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: The United States, China, and the European Union are competing for access to platinum-group metals, manganese, and other minerals, increasing pressure on Pretoria to align supply chains geopolitically.

frictionVectors.title: VULNERABLE OIL EXPORT CORRIDOR
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's crude exports depend on pipelines and terminals in war-affected Sudan, leaving production exposed to sabotage, transit bargaining, and external security influence.

frictionVectors.title: ELITE CONTROL OF RESOURCE REVENUES
frictionVectors.details: Oil revenues remain concentrated among political and military networks while fiscal weakness and insecurity limit state oversight, reinforcing dependence on foreign operators and intermediaries.

highlights: Gold and ports draw external powers

frictionVectors.title: GOLD WAR ECONOMY
frictionVectors.details: Competing military networks and foreign-linked traders use gold exports to finance the conflict, weakening central control and deepening external leverage over Sudan's resource base.

frictionVectors.title: RED SEA PORT COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: The struggle over Port Sudan and future maritime access involves regional and extra-regional actors, making transport infrastructure a central instrument of wartime influence.

highlights: Ports and LNG regain strategic focus

frictionVectors.title: LNG DEVELOPMENT BARGAIN
frictionVectors.details: Planned gas investment could expand state revenues and energy security, but contract terms, local-content demands, and foreign control of technology remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: CORRIDOR INFRASTRUCTURE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, and other foreign-backed projects around ports, railways, and logistics corridors improve connectivity while creating long-term questions about debt, concessions, and strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND TRANSIT LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé is a critical gateway for the Sahel, but its expansion depends heavily on foreign capital, shipping networks, and external commercial partners.

frictionVectors.title: NORTHERN BORDER INSECURITY
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist spillover from Burkina Faso threatens transport corridors and state control in northern Togo, increasing reliance on regional and international security assistance.

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and financing pressure
frictionVectors.details: European financial and political support remains closely tied to migration management, giving Brussels significant leverage over Tunisian policy. Tunisia resists formalized external conditionality while facing persistent fiscal stress.

frictionVectors.title: Energy import vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on imported hydrocarbons and electricity exposes Tunisia to price shocks and regional supply disruptions. Renewable projects may improve resilience but remain reliant on foreign capital and technology.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP financing and sovereignty disputes
frictionVectors.details: The oil pipeline and upstream projects are backed by major foreign investors, notably TotalEnergies and Chinese-linked financing, embedding external interests in Uganda's future energy revenues. Environmental, land-rights, and sanctions-related opposition continues to challenge the project.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese contractors and lenders remain important to transport and energy infrastructure, but debt-servicing obligations reduce Kampala's bargaining flexibility. The government is diversifying partners without eliminating reliance on external capital.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of copper value chains
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is seeking greater domestic processing, transparency, and revenue capture while relying on multinational capital and technology to expand copper production. Competition among Chinese, Gulf, Western, and regional investors gives Lusaka more options but does not remove structural dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Rail and export-route vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Copper exports depend heavily on congested and politically exposed corridors through neighboring states. New rail and Lobito Corridor links could improve diversification, but implementation remains vulnerable to financing and regional security risks.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lithium, platinum, gold, and other mineral projects attract Chinese, Russian, and Western-linked capital, while Zimbabwe struggles to secure local refining and transparent revenue capture. Export restrictions and beneficiation demands have increased state leverage but have not displaced foreign dominance of finance and technology.

frictionVectors.title: Electricity and transmission constraints
frictionVectors.details: Chronic power shortages constrain mining and manufacturing, increasing reliance on imported electricity, private generation, and foreign-funded energy projects. This weakens Zimbabwe's ability to extract full value from its mineral base.
